newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Bomb threat made against Australia's Snowy River dam.
newsitem.headline: Bomb threat made against Australia's Snowy River dam.

text.p: Australian police said on Thursday a bomb threat had been made against a major dam as part of the fight to save Australia's most famous river, the Snowy River, which has dried to a trickle in parts.

The threat to blow up the Jindabyne Dam, which has a capacity three times the size of Sydney Harbour, was made on Tuesday by telephone to the Snowy Mountains Authority, which operates the dam as part of a major hydro-electricity scheme.
"This is a serious threat and we have stepped up security around the dam," said Josephine Kneipp, a spokeswoman for the Snowy Mountains Authority,
"Access has been restricted to the dam and we have modified our security," Kneipp told Reuters by telephone from Jindabyne, 300 kms (184 miles) south of Sydney.

Kneipp said the dam, which is made of rockfill and is 72 metres high (236 feet) and 335 metres long (1,099 feet), is presently quite low, but if destroyed would still cause major flooding, but only minor disruption to electricity generation.

Police inspector Tony Floor told Reuters that the threat was made by a man who identified himself as a member of the "Let The Snowy River Flow. "The caller threatened to blow up the dam wall unless there was greater flow," Floor said.

Writer Andrew Barton "Banjo" Paterson immortalised the river with his late 19th century poem "The Man From Snowy River", which tells of a roaring river fed by melting snow and of a tough mountain rider who beats the country's best horsemen to recover a valuable colt.
The river was dammed in 1967, creating a reservoir with a capacity of 690 billion litres (151 billion gallons) for a massive hydro-electricity system for the states of New South Wales and Victoria.
But landholders downstream have been campaigning for greater waterflow from the dam, arguing the country's most famous river is ankle deep in parts and dying.

They say the river in mountainous country once famous for its wild horses, and which hosts the country's major snow resorts, is facing ecological collapse without a guaranteed 28 percent of the original flow.
Mountain horsemen, downstream landholders and Aborigines staged a horseback protest in Sydney last month.
The Snowy River Alliance on Thursday rejected the threat to the dam, saying many people who are fighting to save the Snowy River would be killed if the dam was destroyed.

"We do not support acts of terrorism, even if they are only threats," Alliance chairman Paul Leete told Reuters. "There is a lot of frustration but not to this level. If the dam was destroyed people downstream, like my family, would be killed."
